topics.title: Design Coffee Vending Machine
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a coffee vending machine that serves espresso, cappuccino, latte and so on. Each drink consumes ingredients (water, milk, beans, sugar). The machine takes payment, checks inventory, brews, returns change and reports low stock. It tests **State** (machine modes), **Factory** (beverages from recipes) and inventory consistency.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Show the menu with prices. Only drinks with enough ingredients are selectable.
- Accept coins, notes or card. Return change or refund on cancel or failure.
- Deduct ingredients and dispense. A technician can refill and go into maintenance mode.
- Alert when an ingredient drops below a threshold.

**Non-functional**
- One transaction at a time; button presses while dispensing are rejected cleanly.
- Never keep money without dispensing: every failure path ends in a dispense or a refund.
- New drinks, recipes and payment methods plug in without touching the core flow.
- Recovers to a safe state after a power cut mid-transaction.

## 1. Scope and chosen solution

I implement one machine with a menu, ingredient stock, coins, cancellation and maintenance. `VendingMachine` serializes sessions; `Recipe` is immutable quantities; `Inventory` reserves resources; a `ChangePlanner` solves bounded coin selection. I keep device and payment results outside domain assumptions.

## 2. Vend algorithm and transitions

```text
select(productId) -> price and recipe
fund(sessionId,coin/payment) -> accepted credit
vend(sessionId) -> COMPLETE | FAILED | DELIVERY_UNCERTAIN
IDLE -> SELECTED -> FUNDED -> DISPENSING -> COMPLETE
```

Before DISPENSING I atomically reserve ingredients, a cup and change, then persist the vend identity. A ₹30 drink funded by ₹50 reserves ₹20 change before brewing. Known pre-brew failure refunds/releases untouched resources; after partial brewing I record consumed stock and waste, not a fictitious rollback. Device uncertainty blocks automatic repeat dispensing until reconciled. With 95 g beans, 1,000 ml water and 20 cups, a 10 g/150 ml recipe permits six servings. Maintenance rejects new sessions and records operator stock/cash adjustments without overwriting history.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![Design Coffee Vending Machine: VendingMachine owns VendSession; VendSession selects Recipe; Recipe reserves from Inventory; VendSession reserves change ChangePlanner; VendSession dispenses through DispenserPort; VendSession collects through PaymentPort](designs/lld-11.svg)](designs/lld-11.svg)

The **recipe** describes ingredient quantities, **inventory** records available ingredients, and a **vend session** owns one customer's interaction. A state machine answers which actions are allowed at each stage: inserting money during maintenance must not accidentally start brewing.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![Reserve ingredients and change before committing the physical action.](lessons/lld-11-flow.svg)

*Reserve ingredients and change before committing the physical action.*

![Physical evidence determines whether retry or refund is appropriate.](lessons/lld-11-failure.svg)

*Physical evidence determines whether retry or refund is appropriate.*

### Worked calculation and implementation

A recipe requiring 10 g beans and 150 ml water allows `min(beans/10, water/150, cups)` servings. With 95 g beans, 1,000 ml water and 20 cups, water limits capacity to six drinks. Inventory checks must reserve the whole recipe together; separately decrementing beans and then discovering no cup leaves inconsistent stock.

```text
VendSession: IDLE -> SELECTED -> FUNDED -> DISPENSING -> COMPLETE
Failures: SELECTED/FUNDED -> CANCELLED
          DISPENSING -> DELIVERY_UNCERTAIN -> RECONCILIATION
```

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Key abstractions

| Type | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `VendingMachine` | Context and facade; holds the current `MachineState` |
| `MachineState` | `Idle`, `Selecting`, `PaymentPending`, `Dispensing`, `Maintenance` |
| `Beverage` / `Recipe` | name, price, `Map<Ingredient, Integer>` quantities |
| `BeverageFactory` | `create(type)` builds a beverage from the recipe registry |
| `Inventory` | `hasEnough(recipe)`, `deduct(recipe)` (atomic), `refill` |
| `PaymentHandler` | Strategy: `CoinPayment`, `CardPayment`; change calculation |
| `InventoryObserver` | Low-stock alert |

```java
class Inventory {
    private final Map<Ingredient, Integer> stock = new EnumMap<>(Ingredient.class);
    synchronized boolean tryDeduct(Recipe r) {
        if (!r.needs().entrySet().stream().allMatch(e -> stock.get(e.getKey()) >= e.getValue())) return false;
        r.needs().forEach((ing, q) -> stock.merge(ing, -q, Integer::sum));
        return true;
    }
}
```

### Design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Recipes as data.** Don't make `Cappuccino extends Coffee` with hard-coded quantities. A recipe registry (loaded from config) plus a Factory means a new drink is a config entry. Use a Decorator only for user add-ons (extra shot, extra sugar).

**2. Check and deduct atomically.** "Check, then deduct" as two calls races if two dispense paths exist. A single `tryDeduct` under a lock is all-or-nothing.

**3. When to deduct versus when to charge.** Order: confirm availability, collect payment, reserve and deduct ingredients, dispense. If dispensing fails, refund and restore ingredients. Never take money for a drink you can't make.

**4. State pattern.** In `Maintenance`, selections are rejected. In `Dispensing`, cancel is rejected. Each state handles only its legal events.

**5. Menu availability is derived.** Recompute which drinks are selectable from inventory after every deduct or refill, and push that to the display (Observer).

### Ownership, boundaries and invariants

**Central design question:** Inventory reservation, money acceptance and physical dispensing are separate observable steps.

Machine owns SlotInventory and a VendSession. Product describes a SKU; Recipe or Selection maps it to ingredients when appropriate. PaymentAcceptor tracks tender; ChangePolicy selects available denominations; DispenserPort reports success or jam. RefundJournal records incomplete recovery.

**Correctness rule:** Never decrement sellable stock twice for one vend request. Do not claim successful delivery before the hardware confirms it. Accepted money must end in purchase, change, refund or an explicit recoverable balance.

```text
slot(id,sku,available,reserved); vend(id,sku,price_minor,tender_minor,state); cash(denomination,count)
```

### End-to-end execution trace

Select a product; validate stock and price; reserve stock; accept sufficient tender; verify change availability; journal the vend; dispense; on confirmation consume stock and return change; on jam reverse the reservation and initiate refund.

### Concurrency and recovery walkthrough

Two sessions select the last unit while an operator restocks. One inventory owner serializes reserve/commit/release; restocking must not overwrite reserved counts. Network payment callbacks use the vend operation ID.

### Policy choices and extension seams

State is helpful for selection/payment/dispense transitions. Different products can use Strategy for preparation. Do not let product factories control cash or mutate global inventory.

### Edge cases that change the design

Enough total money does not imply the machine can make change. Power loss after dispensing needs journal reconciliation. A refund actuator can fail too, so expose an operator-review state instead of looping forever.

**Topic-specific cases:** Last-item race; exact change; impossible change; jam; duplicate confirmation; refund failure; restart during dispense.

### Further reading

- [Java 21 concurrency contracts](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html) — synchronization and executor semantics.
- [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) — database guarantees differ from process locks.

### Work through the important decisions

Coin selection is a bounded change problem: available denominations and counts matter. A ₹20 difference does not prove a ₹20 coin is present. Reserve a feasible change plan before consuming money, or show an exact-change policy before purchase.

Once hot water has entered a cup, cancelling cannot restore the original ingredients. Record consumed quantities and waste; do not “roll back” physical brewing by incrementing every ingredient counter. Maintenance mode should block new sessions and reconcile cash/stock under an operator identity.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Does a new drink require another machine state?** Usually no. A new recipe changes data; new physical behaviour may need a new dispenser strategy.

**Can a failed sensor mean zero delivery?** Not necessarily. Distinguish known none from unknown.

## 7. Closing answer

I reserve a complete recipe and feasible change plan before vending. Session state distinguishes financial acceptance from physical delivery, and unknown dispense outcomes require evidence rather than an automatic second drink. Recipes are data; hardware and payment are explicit adapters.

topics.title: Google Search
topics.concepts: Crawling, indexing, inverted index, ranking, distributed search
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design web search like Google, at a high level. Asha types **"spring boot rate limiter"** and, in about 200 ms, gets ten relevant pages with titles and short snippets – chosen from billions of pages on the web.

Search has two halves: an offline half that crawls the web and builds an index, and an online half that answers queries from that index very fast.

## Requirements

- Crawl billions of web pages and keep them reasonably fresh.
- Build an index that maps words to the pages containing them.
- Answer keyword queries with the top 10 results, titles and snippets, in about 200 ms.
- Rank results by relevance and page quality.
- Handle about 100,000 queries per second.

## Step 1: Clarify the requirements

> **💡 Tip**
> Say up front that you will split the design into crawl → index → serve. Interviewers want to see that separation.

**Candidate:** How many pages should we index?

**Interviewer:** About 10 billion.

**Candidate:** How fresh must results be?

**Interviewer:** News within minutes would be nice; most pages within days or weeks is fine.

**Candidate:** Query volume?

**Interviewer:** About 100,000 queries a second at peak.

**Candidate:** Do we need images, maps, ads, spelling correction?

**Interviewer:** No. Plain web results.

**Candidate:** How sophisticated should ranking be?

**Interviewer:** Explain the main signals; no machine-learning deep dive.

**Functional requirements**

1. Crawl pages politely and repeatedly.
2. Build an inverted index.
3. Serve ranked top-10 results with snippets.

**Non-functional requirements**

1. Query latency about 200 ms.
2. Always available; a slightly stale index is acceptable.
3. Index billions of pages across thousands of machines.

## Step 2: Estimate the scale

> **💡 Tip**
> Size the crawl and the index separately. They are different problems.

**Crawling**

```text
Pages                 = 10 billion
Refresh every ~10 days → 1 billion pages per day ≈ 11,600 pages per second
Average page          ≈ 100 KB HTML → about 1.2 GB/s of downloads
```

What it means: crawling is a large distributed job with thousands of fetchers.

**Index**

```text
Text per page after cleaning   ≈ 10 KB
Raw text                       = 10B × 10 KB  = 100 TB
Inverted index (compressed)    ≈ 30–50% of text ≈ 30–50 TB
```

What it means: the index does not fit on one machine; it must be split into shards, and each shard copied for query throughput.

## Step 3: Define the API

```http
GET /v1/search?q=spring+boot+rate+limiter&page=1
→ 200 {
  "results": [
    { "url": "https://…", "title": "Rate limiting in Spring Boot…", "snippet": "…use a token bucket…" }
  ],
  "estimatedTotal": 1840000
}
```

> **🎯 In the interview**
> The public API is tiny. The interesting design is behind it: how the index is built and how one query fans out to many machines.

## Step 4: Define the data model

| Store | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| URL frontier | URLs to fetch, priority, next fetch time, per-host queues |
| Document store | url, fetched HTML/text, fetch time, content hash |
| Inverted index (per shard) | term → posting list of (docId, positions, term frequency) |
| Document metadata | docId → url, title, PageRank score, language |
| Index generations | which index version each shard is currently serving |

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Split the index **by document** (each shard holds all terms for a subset of pages). A query goes to every shard, each returns its own top results, and a broker merges them. This keeps shards independent and balanced.

## Step 5: Draw the high-level design

[![High-level design: the crawler frontier feeds fetch-and-parse workers that store documents; index builders turn documents into index generations; the query broker sends each query to all index shards and the rank-and-snippets stage returns the top results.](designs/hld-11.svg)](designs/hld-11.svg)

**Offline: crawl and index**

1. The **frontier** holds URLs to fetch, ordered by priority and grouped by host.
2. **Fetchers** download pages, respecting `robots.txt` and a polite rate per site.
3. **Parsers** extract text, title and links; new links go back into the frontier.
4. **Index builders** turn documents into posting lists and publish a new **index generation** to the shards.

**Online: answer a query**

1. Asha's query reaches a **broker**, which normalises it to terms: `spring`, `boot`, `rate`, `limiter`.
2. The broker sends the query to every index shard (one replica of each).
3. Each shard intersects the posting lists, scores matches and returns its top 10.
4. The broker merges the shards' lists, picks the overall top 10, and fetches snippets.

![Animation: a query is split into four terms; the broker fans it out to every index shard; each shard intersects posting lists and returns its own top ten; the broker merges them into one global top ten and adds snippets.](learning-figures/hld-11-query.gif)

## Step 6: Go deep

### The inverted index

A book's index maps a word to page numbers. A search index does the same: each term points to a sorted list of the documents that contain it.

```text
spring   → [3, 17, 42, 108, 977, …]
boot     → [17, 42, 300, 977, …]
limiter  → [42, 977, 5120, …]
```

For "spring boot limiter", walk the sorted lists together and keep documents present in all of them: 42 and 977. Because the lists are sorted, this intersection is fast and needs no random access.

[![Inverted index: documents are split into terms; each term maps to a sorted posting list of document IDs; a query intersects the posting lists of its terms and only the shared documents are scored.](learning-figures/hld-11-index.svg)](learning-figures/hld-11-index.svg)

### Ranking: the scoring algorithm

Each candidate document gets a score from several signals:

- **Text relevance (BM25):** the query words appear often in this page and are rare across the web; title matches count more.
- **Link authority (PageRank):** many good pages link to it.
- **Freshness, language, location** and – at Google's scale – machine-learned models over hundreds of signals.

### Crawling politely and efficiently

**Option 1: A single global queue of URLs.**

- Good: simple.
- Problem: fetchers hammer one popular site, and important pages wait behind junk.

**Option 2: A frontier with per-host queues and priorities.**

- Good: one connection per host at a polite rate; important or fast-changing pages are fetched more often.
- Problem: more bookkeeping.

> **⚖️ Design choice**
> Per-host queues with priorities. News front pages are revisited every few minutes; a rarely changing page every few weeks. Content hashes detect duplicate pages so they are indexed once.

> **⚠️ Common mistake**
> Updating the live index in place while queries read it. A query could see half of a shard's new data. Build a new index generation, then switch shards to it atomically.

### Serving fast

Every shard has several replicas, so 100,000 queries a second are spread across copies. Popular queries ("weather", "cricket score") are cached at the broker. If one shard is slow, the broker can return results from the others rather than wait – slightly less complete, but on time.

## Step 7: Find bottlenecks and failure points

| What fails | What happens | How we handle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A site blocks or slows our crawler | Fetches fail | Respect robots.txt and back off per host |
| Crawler traps (infinite calendars) | Endless URLs | Limit depth and URLs per host; detect patterns |
| One index shard is slow | Every query waits for it | Replicas, hedged requests, and a time budget per shard |
| Index build has a bug | Bad results everywhere | Validate a generation before switching; keep the previous one to roll back |
| Popular query spike | Hot load | Result cache at the broker |

## Putting it together

- **Crawl:** prioritised, polite frontier → fetch → parse → new links.
- **Index:** documents → posting lists → a new generation, switched atomically.
- **Serve:** broker fans out to all shards → each scores its top 10 → merge → snippets.

## Interviewer follow-ups

**Why shard by document rather than by term?** With term sharding, a popular term's shard becomes a hotspot and multi-word queries must gather huge lists across machines. Document sharding keeps every shard's work similar.

**How do you get news into results within minutes?** A small, frequently rebuilt "fresh" index alongside the big one; the broker queries both.

**How do you handle typos?** A spelling-correction step before search, using query logs and edit distance.

**How do you make the result page fast?** Cache popular queries, pre-compute snippets where possible, and stop waiting for slow shards after the time budget.

## Wrap up

We crawled politely into a document store, built an inverted index in versioned generations, and answered queries by fanning out to all shards and merging their top results.

> **📝 Key takeaways**
> - Offline crawl and index; online serve. Keep them separate.
> - An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of documents.
> - Shard by document; the broker merges each shard's top results.
> - Rank with text relevance plus link authority and other signals.

## Going deeper (optional)

The detailed version shows how index generations are published so no query ever sees a half-built posting list.

[![Query serving reads a published index generation rather than crawling on demand.](lessons/hld-11-flow.svg)](lessons/hld-11-flow.svg)

Further reading: [Brin and Page – The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine](http://infolab.stanford.edu/~backrub/google.html) and [Google – How Search works](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/).

## Closing answer

"I split search into crawl, index and serve. A frontier with per-host queues and priorities feeds polite fetchers that respect robots.txt; parsers extract text and links, and new links go back into the frontier. Index builders turn documents into an inverted index – each term maps to a sorted posting list – sharded by document and published as versioned generations. At query time a broker sends the terms to every shard; each intersects posting lists, scores candidates with BM25, PageRank and other signals, and returns its top ten. The broker merges them, adds snippets and caches popular queries. Replicas and time budgets keep latency near 200 ms."

topics.title: Production RAG
topics.concepts: Chunking, metadata, hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Take RAG from demo to production: the techniques that move answer quality from "sometimes right" to dependable. That means smarter chunking with metadata, hybrid search, re-ranking, query rewriting and expansion, context compression, freshness and access control, and evaluation-driven tuning, plus how Spring AI's modular RAG components map onto them.

## Requirements

- Advanced chunking (structure-aware, parent-child, contextual headers).
- Hybrid lexical + semantic retrieval and rank fusion.
- Re-ranking with cross-encoders or LLM rankers.
- Query transformation: rewriting, multi-query, HyDE, conversational compression.
- Operational concerns: incremental ingestion, dedup, ACLs, evals and monitoring.

## 1. Selected production pipeline

I choose hybrid retrieval, optional reranking, bounded evidence packing and a typed cited-answer validator. Every answer records source revisions, prompt/model/index versions and a request trace. Current authorization applies before exposure, while index cleanup can remain asynchronous within the lifecycle contract.

## 2. Execution and measurable acceptance

```text
Question -> authorize -> lexical/vector retrieval -> fuse/rerank
         -> pack source spans -> generate -> validate citations/support
Result: SUPPORTED | INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE | CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE | FAILURE
Cache scope: tenant + permission/freshness + corpus/prompt/model versions
```

For 100 answerable cases, retrieving relevant evidence for 85 gives recall 85%; 75 supported final answers give end-to-end success 75%, and conditional generation success 75/85≈88.2%. I also evaluate unanswerable questions; otherwise a system that fabricates every missing answer can look strong. Revoked/deleted sources and conflicting revisions form independent critical slices.

I change chunking, embedding model, fusion, reranking or prompting one at a time against that corpus. Increasing k can add contradictions and token cost, so it is accepted only if measured support improves. Failed queries retain inspectable candidate/selected source IDs without dumping confidential text into general logs. A cached answer is reused only when permission and evidence freshness still match; semantic question similarity does not establish that equivalence.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![Production RAG: Source lifecycle published scope Hybrid retriever; Hybrid retriever candidates Reranker; Reranker ranked passages Evidence packer; Evidence packer bounded evidence Generation; Generation claims citations Claim validator; Evaluation and traces measures recall Hybrid retriever; Evaluation and traces measures support Claim validator](designs/ai-11.svg)](designs/ai-11.svg)

**Recall@k** measures whether relevant evidence appears among retrieved candidates. A **reranker** reorders candidates with a more expensive relevance judgement. **Groundedness** evaluates whether the answer is supported by selected evidence. Improve the failing stage instead of blindly increasing every limit.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![Each stage leaves evidence for diagnosis and versioned evaluation.](lessons/ai-11-flow.svg)

*Each stage leaves evidence for diagnosis and versioned evaluation.*

![Evidence lifecycle extends beyond the primary document store.](lessons/ai-11-failure.svg)

*Evidence lifecycle extends beyond the primary document store.*

### Trace and calculate quality

On 100 answerable questions, relevant evidence may appear for 85. If 75 of those produce supported answers, retrieval recall is 85% while supported end-to-end success is 75% on that set. The conditional generation success is 75/85, about 88.2%. These diagnose different problems; one “accuracy” number hides them.

Reserve a separate unanswerable set. A system that confidently answers every question can score well on answer-present cases while failing dangerously when evidence is missing. Evaluate abstention precision/recall and critical security failures separately.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Mechanism and rationale

**Design question:** What turns a successful RAG demo into a dependable multi-tenant documentation product?

Production RAG is a lifecycle of ingestion, revisioning, retrieval, authorization, evaluation and operations. Hybrid search retrieves lexical and semantic candidates; reranking orders a small candidate set; context assembly removes duplicates and respects token budget.

### Architecture and contracts

```text
Source connector -> revision/ACL capture -> parse/chunk/embed -> staged index -> retrieval -> authorization -> rerank -> citation generation -> support verification

Application contracts (design outline):
IngestRun(sourceRevision,chunkerVersion,indexVersion,status); AnswerTrace(queryId,evidenceIds,promptVersion,modelVersion)
```

Use a simple QuestionAnswerAdvisor path as a baseline, then application-owned retrieval/reranking when policy requires it. Do not copy unversioned advisor constructors into a pinned build.

### Worked reasoning and capacity example

Assume 100 queries/s x 8 retrieved chunks x 600 tokens = 480,000 evidence tokens/s before history and output. Reranking all corpus chunks is impossible; first-stage retrieval must bound the candidate pool.

### Java and Spring AI implementation outline

```java
record RetrievalTrace(String queryId, String indexVersion,
    java.util.List<String> evidenceIds, String promptVersion) {}
// Log identities and counts, not raw private passages by default.
```

### Design decisions and alternatives

Evaluate retrieval failures before adding a larger model. Track data freshness and ACL updates as first-class work. Cache keys include tenant, permitted corpus version, prompt/model version and query normalization.

### Failure scenario and safe recovery

A shared semantic answer cache serves a correct answer to a user lacking access to the supporting documents. Partition caches by authorization domain and verify access on hits; similarity alone is not a safe cache key.

### Security, privacy and provenance

A more complex pipeline can be harder to debug and less reliable. Keep a measurable baseline and change one retrieval/generation component at a time.


**Verification criteria:** Supported-answer rate, retrieval recall, citation correctness, abstention, p99 latency, indexing freshness and unauthorized evidence exposure. Slice metrics by tenant, language and document type.

### Further reading

- [Spring AI 1.1 ChatClient and request APIs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/chatclient.html).
- [Spring AI tool-execution boundary](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/tools.html).
- [MCP specification, versioned protocol concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18).
- [Original RAG research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) and [Transformer research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) for background rather than framework instructions.

### Work through release changes

Change one variable at a time: chunking, embedding model, hybrid weights, reranker or prompt. Version the corpus and expected evidence, then compare by topic, document age, language and answerability. A larger k increases latency/context and may add contradictory evidence; it is not an automatic quality improvement.

Cache keys need tenant, permission/freshness scope and relevant corpus/prompt/model versions. Similar questions are not sufficient grounds for sharing answers across users. Preserve source spans in traces so support review can inspect a claim without rerunning today's changed index.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Should generation be blamed when the source was never retrieved?** First diagnose retrieval; the generator cannot reliably cite missing evidence.

**Is a retrieval score a confidence score for the final answer?** No.

## 7. Closing answer

Production RAG is a lifecycle and quality pipeline, not one vector lookup. I version sources and components, measure evidence recall separately from answer support, and enforce current permissions even when indexes or caches lag. Release decisions use critical-case gates and inspected regressions.
